The reach difference is a fact about two fixed catalogues: one system put ten distinct items into fifty slots and the other put five, and no amount of re-running changes that, so it is the firmer finding. The hit-rate difference is 0.68 against 0.60 on fifty trials, which is 1.1547 standard errors apart with a standard error of 0.069282, and the plausible band around the baseline at the conventional 95 per cent runs from 0.464207 to 0.735793, which contains the first system's figure. The third option collapses that distinction. The second invents a target for coverage, since a reach figure is a measurement rather than a quota, and padding is exactly what it is supposed to detect. The fourth treats the two figures as rivals when they answer different questions and are only meaningful side by side.

questions.topic: A user and an item the system has never seen
questions.learningObjective: pair a cold-start case with the evidence a remedy is allowed to use
questions.stem: A catalogue serves a film released this morning and a customer who registered this morning, neither with any history. Three remedies are proposed. Which pairing of remedy and justification holds up?

options.text: Infer both from the time of day each appeared, since a release and a registration at the same hour indicate the same underlying taste
options.misconception: invents a signal in a timestamp

options.text: Describe the film by its own attributes and place the customer among people whose early behaviour resembles theirs, because both fallbacks borrow evidence from outside the subject itself
Show the most popular items to both, because a subject with no history has no information to contribute and popularity is the only remaining signal
options.misconception: treats the fallback as the whole answer, ignoring that the film's own attributes are available

options.text: Wait until each has a history, because any answer given before then is a guess that will damage the relationship
options.misconception: believes withholding an answer is safer than giving a weak one

questions.explanation: A cold start is an absence of one kind of evidence, not of all evidence, and the remedy has to name which evidence remains. For the film, its own attributes are present and untainted, so it can be placed among films people with similar descriptions liked, which is a description-based fallback rather than a history-based one. For the customer, what is present is their first session, so they can be placed among people whose earliest behaviour resembles it, and that is a weaker claim about them than a settled history would support. The second option stops at popularity, which is the correct last resort and a poor first choice for a film whose attributes carry real information. The third treats abstention as the safe option, and it is the more expensive one: a new customer shown nothing has no reason to come back and generate the history the system was waiting for, so the cold start reproduces itself. questions.topic: The measure a stated interface deserves
questions.learningObjective: pair a stated interface with the evaluation that reflects how its results are used
questions.stem: A catalogue is about to choose the single number it will be judged on. Two candidates are on the table: a hit rate over trials, and a normalised gain at the fourth position. Which pairing of measure and justification holds up?

options.text: The normalised gain at four, because four results are what a user is shown and the measure prices the ones near the top, which is where a change in the model shows up
The hit rate, because it does not depend on where in the list a wanted item appeared and so measures whether the system works at all
options.misconception: prefers a measure that is blind to the only variable the interface controls

options.text: The normalised gain at four, because four is the largest number of results the interface will ever show and a measure should use the largest available list
options.misconception: justifies the cut-off by the largest list rather than by what users read

options.text: The hit rate, because a normalised gain assumes the relevance grades are right and this catalogue's assessors agree only three times in five
options.misconception: uses assessor disagreement to dismiss a measure without checking what the hit rate assumes

questions.explanation: The measure has to describe the decision the system is actually part of. If four results are shown, then what matters is the quality of the first four in order, and a normalised gain at four prices exactly that: it is sensitive to a wanted item moving from fourth to first, and a change in the model that improves the ordering without changing the set of four will show up in it and in no other figure. A hit rate counts whether a wanted item was in the list at all, so a retriever that returns the right four items in the wrong order and one that returns them in the right order score identically, which makes it blind to the only thing the ranking controls. The third option confuses the largest list that could be shown with the list that is shown. The fourth raises a real concern, since disagreement between assessors adds noise to any graded measure, but the answer does not follow: a hit rate is computed from the same judgements and inherits the same noise, so the objection cuts against both candidates equally and argues for more careful marking rather than for the blunter measure.
questions.hint: Ask what the interface shows and what the system controls, then pick the measure that responds to that.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What leaving one cell out is taken to prove
questions.learningObjective: explain what a leave-one-out evaluation assumes about the cells it did not leave out
questions.stem: Explain what a leave-one-out evaluation of a recommender assumes, and give the sentence that gets the limitation wrong.

answer.exemplar: Leaving one cell out at a time and predicting it from the rest assumes two things, and the first is the one that breaks first. It assumes that the cell it removed is the only information the prediction could have used, which is true of the average and of the low-rank fit and false of anything that reads the user's whole history, because the same user's other cells and the same item's other users are still in the training set. That is the mechanism behind a leaked figure: on three held-out cells whose predictions were 2.6, 4.2 and 3.9 against truths of 4, 3 and 5, a clean construction gives a mean absolute error of 1.233333 and one that left the target cell in the profile gives 0.833333, so the leak cuts the error by a third. The second assumption is that the cells are exchangeable, that any one of them could have been the one left out, which is what lets the average over all of them stand for performance on a cell nobody has rated yet. The sentence that gets it wrong is the one that says leave-one-out removes the influence of the answer, because it removes the answer from one average and not from the neighbours that supplied the prediction. A related wrong sentence says the procedure is unbiased because every cell is predicted once, which confuses being computed for every cell with being independent of every cell.

questions.explanation: The two assumptions fail in different ways and only one of them is usually noticed. The information assumption is a leak: anything the model derives from the target row or column, whether directly or through a neighbour's similarity, is still in scope after the cell is nominally removed, and the resulting figure is optimistic in a way that scales with how much the surrounding rows say about the cell. The exchangeability assumption is subtler and cannot be fixed by writing better code: a rating table is not a random sample, so a cell that was never filled is missing because the user never saw the item, which is exactly the situation a recommender is asked about, while a cell that was filled was filled by someone who chose to rate it. An evaluation over filled cells therefore measures performance on an easier and differently-composed population than the one the system serves, and the honest version of the claim is a statement about the filled cells. Both assumptions have to be written down beside the figure, because a leave-one-out number without them is not a performance claim at all.
questions.hint: Ask what else the prediction could read besides the cell that was removed, and whether the cells resemble one another.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two ways of comparing the same pair of vectors
questions.learningObjective: explain why two candidates can swap places when the length is divided out
questions.stem: Explain why a retriever that ranks by the raw dot product and one that ranks by the cosine can return the two candidates in opposite orders, using a query of (1, 0) against candidates of (2, 5) and (1.5, 0).

answer.exemplar: The two measures divide by different things, and one of them divides by a great deal. The dot product with a query of (1, 0) is simply the candidate's first component, so it is 2 for the first candidate and 1.5 for the second, and the first wins. The cosine divides each of those by the candidate's length, and the lengths are 5.385165 and 1.5, so the first candidate's score becomes 0.371391 and the second's becomes 1.0, and the order reverses. The reversal is not a rounding effect: the first candidate's dot product is 1.333333 times the second's while its length is 3.59011 times, so the length more than cancels the advantage. What the raw product is really ranking is a mixture of content and size, and on unnormalised term counts a long document wins simply by being long, which is why a retriever switched from one to the other does not merely rescale its scores but reorders its results. The sentence that gets this wrong is the one that says the cosine is the dot product divided by a constant, which is true only when both candidates have the same length, and in a corpus of documents of different lengths none do. A related wrong sentence claims the reordering is noise, when the two orderings are both deterministic and the difference between them is a property of the data.

questions.explanation: The two measures answer different questions and the difference is systematic rather than incidental. A dot product asks how much of the query's content the candidate contains, weighted by the candidate's size, so it is a measure of content times size. A cosine asks how close the two directions are, so it is a measure of content alone, and the two coincide only for candidates of equal length. The arithmetic here is the clean demonstration: the first candidate contains a third more of the query and is nearly four times as long, so normalising removes more than the extra content added. The practical consequences run in both directions. A retriever on raw counts will have its long documents promoted, which is measurable as a correlation between a document's length and its rank, and switching to the cosine will demote them and change every downstream evaluation. And a team comparing two systems must know which measure each used, because a difference in the reported scores may be a difference in the measure rather than in the retrieval.
questions.hint: Compare the ratio of the two dot products with the ratio of the two lengths.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a popularity comparison can and cannot settle
questions.learningObjective: state the scope of a claim made against a popularity baseline
questions.stem: A recommender reaches a hit rate of 0.68 over fifty trials against 0.60 for showing the five most popular items. Explain what that comparison supports and what it does not, and give the sentence that gets it wrong.

answer.exemplar: It supports one narrow claim and blocks a family of larger ones. The narrow claim is that on these fifty trials the model returned an item the user went on to take more often than the popular-items rule did, by eight hits, a lift of 13.33 per cent. What it does not support is that the model is better, in the sense of having been shown to be better, because with a rate near 0.6 over fifty trials the standard error of a single figure is 0.069282 and the two differ by 1.1547 of those; the band of plausible values around the baseline at the conventional 95 per cent runs from 0.464207 to 0.735793 and contains 0.68 without strain. A run of the baseline that reached 17 or more hits out of 50 would have produced 0.68 by luck. Nor does the comparison say anything about users unlike the fifty, about items outside the catalogue, or about the days the trials were run on, and the coverage figures differ too, with the model reaching ten distinct items and the baseline five. The sentence that gets it wrong is the one that says the model outperformed the baseline by thirteen per cent and is therefore the better model, because a percentage difference between two noisy figures is not an established difference however exactly it is computed. A related wrong sentence says beating the baseline proves the model is personalised, when the baseline is beaten by any system that has learned which items are generally popular, which is a much weaker property than being different for different people.

questions.explanation: A baseline comparison is a floor test and its own power depends on the size of the trial set, which is why the two halves of this claim have to be kept apart. The direction of the difference is established; the size of the difference is not. Reporting a percentage improvement without the count of trials converts a sign into a magnitude the evidence does not carry, and the failure is more common on the winning side because a report is written to announce the result. Three things strengthen the comparison without changing what it means, and all three are worth doing before the number is quoted: more trials, so that the gap is several standard errors rather than one; a paired design in which the same users see both systems, which removes much of the between-user variation; and a report of the interval rather than the point, so a reader can see the overlap for themselves. And a separate question remains after the baseline is beaten, which is whether the gain comes from personalisation or from having learned the popularity distribution better than the baseline did.
questions.hint: Ask how far apart the two figures are compared with how far apart two runs of the same system can land.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: From a pile of text to a ranked list
questions.learningObjective: order the steps that turn a document collection into a weighted, comparable set of vectors
questions.stem: A collection of four short documents is to become a ranked answer to a query. Put these four steps in the order that produces vectors whose weights mean what the report will say they mean.

options.text: Split each document into terms and count them, so that every later step has something to weight
Count in how many documents each term appears, because the weight of a term depends on the whole collection and not on any one document
Multiply each term's count in a document by the logarithm of the collection size over the document count, which turns a count into a weight
Scale each document's vector by its own length, so that a long document does not outrank a short one that matches the query more precisely

questions.explanation: The order is forced by what each step consumes. Counting terms comes first because the weight is a multiplier on a count and there is nothing to multiply until the counts exist. The document count comes second because it is a property of the whole collection, so it cannot be computed while documents are still being read one at a time, and a system that updates it incrementally is the one that ends up with weights that mean something slightly different from the definition in the report. Weighting comes third, and only now does every term in every document have a number that can be compared with another document's. Normalising comes last, because it is a per-document operation that acts on a finished vector, and doing it earlier would make the collection-wide document count depend on how the individual document happened to be tokenised. The failure this ordering prevents is the one that is hardest to see later: a report that says the weight is the logarithm of four over the document count while the code computed it against a running total that included the query is describing a system that does not exist, and on a collection this small the two differ in the third decimal place, which is nowhere near enough to be noticed by reading the code.
questions.hint: Ask what each step needs to have already been computed before it can run.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: From a perfect score to a number someone can believe
questions.learningObjective: order the checks that separate a real retrieval result from one that improved because it was measured on the wrong thing
questions.stem: A retriever reports a precision at three of 1.0 on twelve queries whose answer sets hold three items each, which is a result no production system achieves. Put these four checks in the order that would locate the problem soonest.

options.text: Check whether any query's own text is in the collection, because a retriever that finds a query inside the index will match it perfectly every time
Have a second assessor mark the same queries, because a key written from the retriever's own output reproduces its mistakes as correctness
Re-measure on queries whose answer sets were written after the collection was last rebuilt, since a key assembled from the same vintage as the index is not a test of anything new
Look at the queries themselves, since a perfect score on twelve queries means either the queries or the index contains something the retriever should not have had

questions.explanation: A perfect score is a statement about the measurement before it is a statement about the retriever, and the checks run from the most mechanical to the most procedural. Reading the queries comes first because it is free and because the most common cause of a perfect score is visible in the query text itself: a query that is a sentence lifted from a document in the collection is answered by finding that document. The second check is the specific version of the first and is worth separating because it is a one-line test with a definite answer, and because a collection that contains its own queries is a real condition of many internal search systems. A second assessor comes third, since writing a fresh answer key is a day's work and is wasted if the problem was mechanical, and it is the check that catches a key assembled by asking the old retriever what it would have returned. The vintage check is last because it is the most expensive and the most general: it asks whether the evaluation would still pass on material the system had no part in producing, which is the question that matters once the others are clean. Skipping straight to a fresh key is the common mistake, because it is the most reassuring check to run and the least likely to find a bug in the retriever.
questions.hint: Run the checks that are free and mechanical before the ones that cost a day or a rebuild.

The two figures together are the diagnosis: a system that reaches half the catalogue and still spends half its space on three items is recommending broadly and narrowly at once, and any accuracy figure it posts has to be read against that. A single-item share of 0.2 is not by itself alarming, since a genuinely dominant item exists in most catalogues, and the number to watch is whether it is rising. The share is also the quantity that a novelty measure is built from, because a recommendation is novel exactly when it is not one of the items a user has already been shown, and a run that concentrates cannot be novel on average however good its accuracy is.

questions.topic: A gain stated as a proportion rather than a difference
questions.learningObjective: express an error reduction as a proportion of a baseline and read what the choice of denominator does
questions.stem: A mean absolute error of 0.833333 for a constant baseline of 3.5 on held-out ratings of 4, 3 and 5 compares against 0.366667 for a model predicting 3.7, 3.2 and 4.4. As a percentage of the baseline's error, what reduction does the model achieve?
questions.explanation: The absolute reduction is 0.833333 minus 0.366667, which is 0.466667, and expressing it as a proportion of the baseline gives 0.466667 over 0.833333, which is 0.56, or 56 per cent. The denominator is the whole content of the choice, and it is worth seeing what the alternatives do. As a share of the model's own error the same reduction would be 0.466667 over 0.366667, which is 1.272727, or 127 per cent, a figure that is arithmetically correct and rhetorically absurd, since it says the reduction exceeds the thing being reduced. The same pair of errors read on a squared measure gives 57.79 per cent, since the root-mean-square errors are 0.957427 and 0.404145, so the measure and the baseline together move the claim by nearly two points. Three points are worth keeping in view: the baseline of 3.5 is the mean of the three held-out ratings and is therefore the best constant available after seeing the answers, which makes the 56 per cent a conservative figure; the trial set is three cells, so no percentage here is a stable quantity; and a percentage improvement against a named baseline is a claim about that pair of systems rather than about the model in general.
